title: 10 Things I Learned In College
html:
Fall semester starts next week, so all the angsty, anxious, boisterous, loud, and smelly (yes, smelly) undergraduates are swarming campus once again. Oh, how I miss those quiet, empty-gym, summertime mornings.

At the time of writing this, I’m starting my second year as a master’s student, which will likely be my final year of schooling altogether. With my formal education coming to a close, I felt inspired to share some nuggets of wisdom I’ve picked up throughout my years in college—some relating to college, others not. These lessons were hard-earned, as I, for better or for worse, have a tendency of learning things the hard way. Needless to say, my college experience has been rather painful. But, alas, pain is a prerequisite for growth, so I am grateful for it. Hope you enjoy :)

In no particular order:

  1. People need people: Don’t glorify isolation. In the correct dose, isolation can lead to extraordinary personal growth and productivity. In excess, it can lead to depression. Prioritize human connection.

  2. Not fitting in sucks. Fitting in is worse: Acting normal produces normal results. If you don’t want normal results, you need to stop acting normally. When you stop acting normally, you stop fitting in. You choose between relatability and being exceptional.

  3. Going to class is a waste of time: You're probably going to get confused, lost, start day-dreaming, and end up having to re-learn the material using the lecture materials and online resources anyways. Also, self-teaching is an essential skill for life, so you might as well start honing it now. Skip the fuss. Skip class. Self-teach.

  4. Shrink your window of focus to reduce anxiety: Big tasks like completing a degree, a semester, or a project seem daunting when considered in their entirety. But focusing on what needs to be done today makes your workload seem manageable… because it is. You got this.

  5. Sleep: Kevin Kelly said, “If you can’t tell what you desperately need. It’s probably sleep.” He’s right. Nobody is above sleep.

  6. Being kind makes you an outlier: Many people, especially in the midwestern United States, are superficially pleasant. Fewer people, however, deeply care about how they affect those around them. Be kind, and people will notice.

  7. The mate value of a young adult male is approximately zero: In early adulthood, you have no money, no job, no status, no stability, no credentials, and limited earning potential given your current level of education and skill development. It’s no wonder that smart, beautiful, mature women want nothing to do with you. You have nothing to offer them. So study, read books, listen to podcasts, learn stuff, get in shape, get good at something useful so people will pay you good money to do it, and, most importantly, don’t be an asshole along the way. Become someone worth wanting around, and people will start wanting you around.

  8. Don’t lie: Lying corrodes relationships, and there are almost always truths worth telling. Telling uncomfortable truths gives people reason to believe that we mean what we say. This is the foundation of trust. Make your words mean something. Don’t lie.

  9. Smell good: In a variety of my computer science classes, there was enough BO to kill a horse. Interacting with smelly people is unpleasant, so being smelly discourages people from interacting with you. Smelling good might not encourage positive interactions (although it might), but it certainly doesn’t discourage them. For an example of what I mean, see below for a snapshot of a Reddit thread from my university about a computer science course I took. They sell deodorant at Target, folks.

  1. Just ask: If you’re looking for research roles, a teaching assistantship, a job, advice, mints, or squishy cows, just ask. Ask around, send cold emails, talk to your professors, etc.. If you ask for something, the worst that can happen is that you’re told no. Today, I saw some Life Savers mints on a faculty member’s desk. I asked, “Are those Life Savers?” She responded, “Would you like one?” And just like that, I was one mint richer. I then learned that she had a drawer full of squishy cows. “Are you giving them away?” I asked. And just like that, I was one squishy cow richer. So if you want something, just ask. You might be surprised at what follows.
